read.sections.0.text.note: "Hiện vật" for artefact (not in KEY_TERMS). Chosen because it is the usual museum and school word. "Điều quan sát" is used for "an observation" so that the glossary word "quan sát" stays in the text; "một suy luận" for an inference. Check these noun forms are natural.
read.sections.0.text.source: An object that people made or used in the past is called an artefact. When you study an artefact, start with what you can see. An observation is a detail that you can notice for yourself, with your eyes or your hands. The tin has a dent in the lid, the letters "ML" on its side and a repaired hinge. These are all observations. Next, you can make an inference, which is an idea that you build from clues. For example, you might say that the owner used this tin to carry lunch. That could be true, but the tin itself does not tell us.
read.sections.0.text.back: A thing that people made or used in the past is called an artifact. When you study an artifact, start from what you can see. An observation is a detail you notice yourself, with your eyes or your hands. The tin box has a dent in the lid, the two letters "ML" on the side and a repaired hinge. All of those are observations. Next, you can make an inference, that is, an idea you build from the clues. For example, you could say the owner used this box to carry lunch. That might be true, but the box itself does not tell us.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: "Hiện vật", "điều quan sát" and "suy luận" all stay in the simpler text because they are glossary words. Check the simpler text is still easy enough.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: An old object that people used is an artefact. First, look at the artefact. Say what you can see. This is an observation. The tin has a dent. It has the letters ML. Someone fixed its hinge. Next, you can guess what the clues mean. This is an inference. Maybe the owner carried lunch in the tin. That could be true. But the tin does not tell us.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: An old thing that people used is an artifact. First, look at the artifact. Say what you see. That is an observation. The tin box has a dent. It has two letters, ML. Someone repaired its hinge. Next, you can guess what the clues mean. That is an inference. Maybe the owner carried lunch in the box. That might be true. But the box does not tell us.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Use a second source to test an idea
read.sections.1.heading.back: Use a second source to check an idea

read.sections.1.text.note: "Bối cảnh" for context (KEY_TERMS). "Mối liên hệ" for link. Pronoun "cô" for Mina (a woman named Mina L.); the English uses "her". Check. | Review: Same as above. [Reviewer changed: xếp cơm và đậu → cho cơm và đậu]
read.sections.1.text.source: A second source can help you test an inference. The notebook page says that Mina L. packed rice and beans in her tin before going to a repair workshop. The tin has the letters "ML", so there may be a link between Mina and the tin. This link is worth checking, but it does not prove that the tin was hers. The letters could belong to someone else, and objects often pass from one person to another. Context can help too. Context is the information around an object, such as where it was found. We know the tin and the notebook were found in the same box.
read.sections.1.text.back: A second source can help you check an inference. The notebook page says Mina L. packed rice and beans in her box before going to a repair workshop. The box has the two letters "ML", so there might be a link between Mina and the box. This link is worth checking, but it does not prove the box was hers. The two letters could belong to someone else, and objects are often passed from one person to another. Context can also help. Context is the information around a thing, for example where it was found. We know the box and the notebook were found in the same crate.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Another source can help us check an idea. A notebook says Mina L. packed rice and beans in her tin. The tin has the letters ML. So maybe the tin was hers. But we cannot be sure. ML could stand for another person. People also give things to other people. Context helps us too. Context is what is around the object. The tin and notebook were in the same box.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Another source can help us check an idea. A notebook says Mina L. packed rice and beans in her box. The box has two letters, ML. So maybe the box was hers. But we cannot be sure. ML could be another person's name. People also often give things to other people. Context also helps us. Context is what is around the thing. The box and the notebook lay in the same crate.
read.sections.1.simpler.note: Review: Awkward repeated 'cho'. Native speaker may prefer another verb (đưa, chuyển). [Reviewer changed: xếp cơm và đậu → cho cơm và đậu; 'hay cho đồ cho người khác' → 'hay tặng đồ cho người khác']

read.sections.2.heading.source: Say what you know and what you do not know
read.sections.2.heading.back: Say what you know and what you do not know

read.sections.2.text.note: "Nhãn giới thiệu trong bảo tàng" for "museum labels". "Có thể" and "nhiều khả năng" for "may" and "probably". Check these are the hedging words a Vietnamese museum label would use.
read.sections.2.text.source: A careful historian is honest about uncertainty. The repair shows that someone chose to fix the tin and keep using it. However, it does not prove that the owner was poor or careless, because people repair things for many reasons. Museum labels often use careful words, such as "may" or "probably", when the evidence is not certain. A good label for the tin might say, "This tin may have carried the lunch of someone who worked at a repair workshop." A dated record, or a list of the tin's past owners, could make this claim stronger.
read.sections.2.text.back: A careful historian is always honest about uncertainty. The repair shows that someone chose to fix the box and keep using it. However, that does not prove the owner was poor or careless, because people repair things for many reasons. Introduction labels in museums often use cautious words, like "might" or "most likely", when the evidence is not certain. A good label for the box might say: "This box might have held the lunch of a person who worked at a repair workshop." A document with a date, or a list of people who owned the box, could make this claim stronger.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: "Sự không chắc chắn" (uncertainty) is a glossary word and an abstract noun; kept in the simpler text. Check a learner can follow it.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Be honest about uncertainty. Someone fixed the tin. So someone wanted to keep it. That does not mean the owner was poor. People fix things for many reasons. Use careful words like may and probably. A label could say: This tin may have carried someone's lunch. A record with a date could help us know more.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Be honest about uncertainty. Someone repaired the box. So someone wanted to keep it. That does not mean the owner was poor. People repair things for many reasons. Use cautious words like might and most likely. A label might say: This box might have held someone's lunch. A paper with a date might help us know more.

watch.summary.source: This is the same short video as in Lesson 1. It explains primary sources. These are things made or used at the time you are studying. An object can be a primary source, just like a letter or a diary. An object shows what it is made of. It also shows its marks and repairs. A piece of writing shows what its writer saw or did. In this lesson, the tin is one primary source and the notebook is another. When you put them together, you can build an idea about who used the tin. But finding two things in the same box does not prove they had the same owner. So a careful historian says what can be seen, then makes an inference, and then names what is still unknown.
watch.summary.back: This is a short video like the one in Lesson 1. The video explains primary sources. Those are things made or used at the time you are learning about. An object can be a primary source, like a letter or a diary. An object shows what it was made of. It also shows marks and repairs. A text shows what the writer saw or did. In this lesson, the tin box is a primary source and the notebook is another source. When you put them together, you can build an idea about the person who used the box. But finding two things in the same crate does not prove they have the same owner. So a careful historian says what can be seen, then makes an inference, then names what is still not known.
